title: 23 Lessons I Learned From Robert Greene On Life, Work, and The Sublime
author: Ryan Holiday
summary: Ryan Holiday marks the release of Robert Greene's The Law of the Sublime by sharing twenty-three lessons from nearly twenty years of working for and learning from him, beginning as a research assistant at nineteen. The lessons cover how to treat work and apprenticeship (value learning over money, be useful, be generous with credit), how to think (keep digging for better sources, develop intuition, hold two opposing ideas, be loyal to the truth), and how to live (alive time versus dead time, a physical practice, patience, concentrating your forces). A recurring thread is that the slow, tedious process is the point: Greene's warning about AI is that handing off a ten-hour translation struggle would have annihilated the thinking process that built his character. The post ends with memento mori, urging readers to thank the people who shaped them while they still can.
points: Choose the opportunity that will teach you the most over the one that pays the most, and treat access to a master as the real compensation.
A good apprentice makes the mentor's life easier by learning what they need, taking something off their plate and building a complementary skill.
Rigor means refusing the first source that fits, verifying context and holding yourself to a high standard.
Difficult, slow work such as translating by hand or writing on notecards builds depth that AI shortcuts would erase.
Creativity is a lagging indicator of long hours of tedious work, so the real question is whether you are doing the work now.
quotes: Always go to what will teach you the most, not what will pay the most. “In the end,” Robert continues, “by valuing learning above all else, you will set the stage for your creative expansion, and the money will soon come to you.

Robert explained that a good apprentice makes a mentor’s life easier. You figure out what they need. You take something off their plate. You develop a skill that complements theirs. That’s how you earn access.
Don’t settle for the first thing that sort of fits. Keep digging. For a better source, a stronger example, a more thoroughly verified quote. Set high standards, then do the work to meet them.
It’s easier to be patient when nothing is happening though. To turn down a life-changing opportunity? That’s the real test.
What if I had ChatGPT, and I put the passage in there, and it gave me the translation right away? The whole thinking process would have been annihilated right there.
It is not fast, easy, or efficient. And that is the point. Writing things down by hand forces me to engage and struggle with the material for an extended period of time.
Because the world is complicated, ambiguous, paradoxical, and contradictory. Because different situations call for different things. Because everything in life depends on context.
None of us gets unlimited time with the people who have shaped our lives. Pick up the phone, send the note, make the trip—tell them what they mean to you, while you still can.
